lead: Cloud computing is not a thing you can point at. It is a way of selling computing, and "cloud" was a marketing word before it was a technical one. In 2011 the US National Institute of Standards and Technology published a short document, SP 800-145, that turned the word into a test: one definition, five essential characteristics, and a rule that all five must hold at the same time. Engineers, buyers and auditors still use that test to decide whether a service is really a cloud or just a rented server wearing a modern logo.
prereq: You need: the idea of pooled resources from chapter 1.1, and the difference between parallel and distributed systems from chapter 1.2.

blocks.text: The standard definition, in paraphrase, says: cloud computing is a model for enabling on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources — networks, servers, storage, applications and services — that can be rapidly provisioned and released with minimal management effort or service-provider interaction.

Read it in four pieces. Model: a way of organising and selling computing, not a single product. On-demand network access: you reach the resources over a network, at the moment you ask. Shared pool of configurable resources: many customers draw from one stock of hardware that can be reshaped into whatever each needs. Rapidly provisioned and released with minimal management effort: no human at the provider has to act for you to start, and none has to act for you to stop.

The same document then lists five essential characteristics, three service models (software, platform and infrastructure as a service) and four deployment models (private, community, public and hybrid). Those two lists belong to chapter 1.6 and chapter 1.7. The characteristics decide yes or no.
Without a definition, every hosting company is a cloud. With one, a buyer or an examiner can check item by item instead of trusting an adjective.
Each characteristic is a question you ask of the service. The names below are the standard ones.

items: On-demand self-service. You obtain computing capability — server time, storage, a database — by yourself, through a console, a form or an API, without a human at the provider. A developer creating a database at 2 a.m. from a web page is the picture to hold.

Broad network access. The service is reachable over the network by standard mechanisms, from ordinary clients: laptops, phones, tablets. The network may be the public internet or a private link; the test is standard access, not open-to-the-world access.

Resource pooling. The provider's resources are pooled to serve many customers at once, a multi-tenant model. Physical and virtual resources are assigned and reassigned as demand moves between customers. You usually do not know which machine holds your workload; you may be allowed to choose a region or a country.

Rapid elasticity. Capacity can be provisioned and released quickly, sometimes automatically, to match demand. To you the supply looks unlimited and available in any quantity at any time. Think of a results-day surge on an exam portal: fifty servers at 9 a.m., three by noon.

Measured service. Usage is metered at a level that suits the service — storage in GB-months, compute in vCPU-hours, bandwidth in GB, or API calls — and reported to both provider and customer. The meter turns usage into a bill.

blocks.text: Virtualisation is the machinery underneath. Pooling needs a way to slice one physical machine into many isolated pieces and hand those pieces to different customers, and elasticity needs the pieces to be created and destroyed in seconds. That machinery belongs to Unit 3; here you only need the link.
Test the service, not the brochure. Ask what the customer actually does and what the provider actually does.

items: Self-service: can capacity be created with no person at the provider in the loop?
Broad network access: can standard clients reach it over a network from outside one building?
Pooling: are many customers served from one pool of hardware, reassigned as demand shifts between them?
Elasticity: can capacity rise and fall quickly with demand, ideally without a request?
Measured service: is usage metered at a fine grain, reported, and reflected in the bill?
If all five fully hold, it is a cloud by this definition. If any one collapses, it is not.

blocks.text: score = Σ cᵢ for i = 1 to 5, with cᵢ ∈ {0, 0.5, 1}
blocks.where: cᵢ is the credit for characteristic i: 1 if it fully holds, 0.5 if partly, 0 if not. The service is a cloud only when every cᵢ = 1, that is min(cᵢ) = 1. The sum is a convenience score out of 5, not a pass mark — four and a half out of five is still a no.

blocks.text: The habit to build: give a verdict, then give the characteristic that fails. "Not a cloud, because self-service and measured service fail" is an answer. "Not a cloud, it's just hosting" is a guess.

figure.caption: The campus server scored on the five characteristics: only resource pooling earns a half credit, so it gets 0.5 out of 5 (10 percent) and is a hosted facility, not a cloud.

examples.question: A college offers its students a login on one server in the campus data centre. The fee is a flat ₹500 per student per year. The service is reachable only from inside the campus Wi-Fi. Accounts are created by emailing the administrator. Score it against the five essential characteristics and decide whether it is a cloud.
steps: The five characteristics: self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, measured service.
Self-service: accounts are created by a human reading email, so the customer cannot act alone. Credit c₁ = 0.
Broad network access: reachable only from campus Wi-Fi, not from a phone on mobile data. Credit c₂ = 0.
Resource pooling: one server serves many students, so hardware is shared, but there is no pool that shifts between tenants. Credit c₃ = 0.5.
Rapid elasticity: the single server has fixed capacity, so a load of 60 students cannot grow to 600 within a few minutes, and no extra machines are created on demand. Credit c₄ = 0.
Measured service: the fee is flat ₹500 per student per year; nothing is metered per hour, per GB or per request, and no usage report reaches the customer. Credit c₅ = 0.
Total score = 0 + 0 + 0.5 + 0 + 0 = 0.5 out of 5, that is (0.5 ÷ 5) × 100 = 10 percent.
Verdict: not a cloud. One partial credit and four full misses, and the definition needs all five.
examples.answer: Score 0.5 out of 5 (10 percent); the service is a hosted campus facility, not a cloud, because self-service, broad network access, elasticity and measured service all fail outright.

total = sum(credits)
print(total)
print(total / 5 * 100)
print(min(credits))

traps: Calling any virtual machine a cloud. A VM on your laptop fails all five: no provider pool shared with other customers, no network access from standard clients, no elastic capacity, no self-service and no meter. Carving several VMs out of one machine is virtualisation; pooling begins only when those slices are handed to different customers. Recite all five, then judge.

Mixing up pooling and elasticity. Pooling is many tenants sharing one pool at the same moment; elasticity is the size of your slice changing over time. One is about sharing, the other about speed of growth.
Reading broad network access as "open to the public internet". A service behind a corporate VPN still passes, because the test is standard clients and standard mechanisms, not anonymity.
Listing service or deployment models as characteristics. SaaS, PaaS, IaaS and public, private, hybrid, community answer different questions; they are not part of the five.
Accepting four out of five as close enough. The definition is a conjunction: every characteristic must hold. Examiners award the mark for the word "all".

quiz.q: Name the five essential characteristics of cloud computing in the standard definition.
quiz.a: On-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service.

quiz.q: Which document gives the standard definition, and which two lists does it add beside the five characteristics?
quiz.a: NIST SP 800-145. It adds three service models (SaaS, PaaS, IaaS) and four deployment models (private, community, public, hybrid).

quiz.q: Why is resource pooling also called multitenancy, and what does the customer typically not know?
quiz.a: One pool of physical hardware is divided among many customers at the same time; each tenant is isolated from the others. The customer usually does not know which physical machine holds the workload, though a region or country may be selectable.

quiz.q: A vendor sells "cloud storage", but raising the quota needs a support ticket and the service is reachable only from the office LAN. Which characteristics fail, and what is the verdict?
quiz.a: Self-service fails (a human must act) and broad network access fails (one building only). The verdict is not a cloud, whatever the marketing says.

quiz.q: A service signs you up from a web form, works on phones over 4G, runs in three data centres, doubles its servers automatically within a minute of load rise, and bills per API call. Score it against the five characteristics.
quiz.a: Self-service 1, broad network access 1, pooling 1, elasticity 1, measured service 1. Total 5.0 out of 5, min credit 1, so it is a cloud.

quiz.q: Why does measured service matter to elasticity, and not only to the bill?
quiz.a: Elasticity must raise and lower capacity automatically, and an automatic decision needs a live measure of demand — requests per second, queue length, CPU load. Measured service builds that same telemetry and also reports it, so the meter serves two masters: the scaling rule and the bill. Metering and monitoring usually share one stream of measurements, but the bill alone does not scale anything.

quiz.q: A bank runs a private cloud inside its own data centre and argues that broad network access does not apply because nothing touches the internet. Is the argument correct?
quiz.a: No. Broad network access asks for standard network mechanisms and standard client devices, which a bank's internal network provides. Deployment model (private) and characteristic (broad access) are separate questions; all five still apply.

beyond: Not for the exam. The NIST definition is a starting point, not the only vocabulary: ISO/IEC 17788 gives a wider international vocabulary for cloud computing, and newer national and regional schemes add requirements the 2011 document never imagined. Sovereignty and data-location rules now push buyers to ask which country a pool sits in. On the cost side, measured service has grown into a whole practice, FinOps, that manages the meter as a budget.
